**Nuvei in advanced talks to acquire Payoneer for $2.7 billion**

*A deal would combine Nuvei's merchant acquiring with Payoneer's cross-border payout network, creating a vertically integrated competitor in a segment where scale increasingly determines margin.*

Nuvei, the Canadian payments processor taken private by Advent International in 2024, is in advanced talks to buy Payoneer in a transaction valued at approximately $2.7 billion, according to Reuters. The deal would marry Nuvei's card acquiring and alternative payment method processing with Payoneer's established position in cross-border marketplace payouts and B2B payments, particularly in emerging markets.

The timing reflects continued consolidation pressure in cross-border payments. Payoneer has built strong distribution among freelancers, SMEs and marketplace sellers in regions such as South and Southeast Asia, while Nuvei's strength lies in regulated verticals and ecommerce acquiring. Under Advent's ownership, Nuvei has the balance sheet flexibility to pursue acquisitions that a public listing might have constrained.

For European payments firms, the combination is worth watching. Payoneer holds licences across multiple EU jurisdictions and has been expanding its B2B accounts payable and receivable capabilities. A merged entity would compete more directly with the likes of dLocal and Adyen in emerging-market merchant services, while strengthening Nuvei's cross-border treasury and payout infrastructure.

*Sources: [Nuvei in 'advanced' talks over $2.7bn Payoneer acquisition - Reuters](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47890/nuvei-in-advanced-talks-over-27bn-payoneer-acquisition---reuters) — Finextra*

**Santander's Getnet launches agent-initiated payment acceptance for merchants**

*Getnet is the first major bank-owned acquirer to offer merchants the ability to accept payments triggered by AI agents, moving agentic commerce from proof-of-concept to production infrastructure.*

Getnet, Santander's global merchant payments platform, has launched capabilities that allow merchants to accept payments initiated by AI agents. The system enables an AI agent acting on behalf of a consumer or business to authenticate, authorise and complete a transaction without direct human intervention at the point of payment.

This follows ING, Worldline and Mastercard's completion of what they described as Europe's first agentic payment earlier this month. Where that was a controlled demonstration, Getnet's announcement positions the capability as generally available to its merchant base. The distinction matters: agentic commerce requires not just a functioning payment rail but merchant-side acceptance infrastructure, and acquirers are now building that layer.

The practical implications are still emerging. Agent-initiated payments raise questions around authentication, liability and dispute resolution that existing card scheme rules were not designed for. But the pace of announcements from major players suggests the industry expects AI agents to become a meaningful payment initiation channel, and is moving to establish early positions before standards crystallise.

*Sources: [Santander's Getnet helps businesses accept agent-initiated payments](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110084/santanders-getnet-helps-businesses-accept-agent-initiated-payments) — Finextra*

stories.original:
**Lloyds partners with Stripe to deliver payment tools to small businesses**

*Lloyds Banking Group is embedding Stripe's payment technology into its SME banking proposition, a notable instance of a major high-street bank using a fintech's infrastructure rather than building or buying its own.*

Lloyds is working with Stripe to offer a suite of payment tools to its small business customers. The partnership gives Lloyds' SME clients access to Stripe's online payment acceptance, invoicing and payment link capabilities through the bank's existing business banking channels.

The move is striking for what it says about build-versus-partner decisions at large banks. Lloyds has 1.2 million business banking customers. Rather than develop proprietary merchant services or acquire a processor, it has opted to embed an established fintech's stack. This mirrors a broader pattern in which banks act as distribution channels for specialist payment technology, accepting a platform role rather than attempting full vertical integration.

For Stripe, the deal extends its reach into a segment — UK micro and small businesses — where bank relationships still dominate. It also follows the recent loss of the Gov.UK Pay contract to Adyen, making this Lloyds partnership a timely reinforcement of Stripe's UK presence. The arrangement effectively turns Lloyds into a reseller, an increasingly common model but one that carries strategic risk if the bank's payment proposition becomes dependent on a single external provider.

*Sources: [Lloyds deliver new payment tech to SMEs in partnership with Stripe](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47883/lloyds-deliver-new-payment-tech-to-smes-in-partnership-with-stripe) — Finextra*

stories.original:
**Monzo and Fair4All Finance pilot credit card for financially excluded borrowers**

*Monzo's Flex Build card, developed with Fair4All Finance, targets consumers locked out of mainstream credit, testing whether a digital bank can serve this segment profitably where traditional lenders have retreated.*

Monzo has launched a pilot credit product called Flex Build, developed in partnership with Fair4All Finance, aimed at consumers who cannot access standard credit cards. The product is designed as a credit-building tool with lower limits and structured repayment, intended to help users establish or repair a credit history.

The pilot sits at the intersection of two regulatory priorities: financial inclusion and the FCA's broader push toward open finance as a mechanism for better lending decisions. Monzo's existing use of transaction data and open banking feeds to assess affordability gives it a potential advantage in underwriting borrowers that traditional credit scoring would reject. Whether that translates into sustainable unit economics at scale is the open question.

Fair4All Finance, which uses dormant assets funding to support financial inclusion, has backed similar initiatives before, but this is its most prominent partnership with a digital bank. The product's success or failure will be closely watched as a signal of whether fintechs can profitably serve excluded segments, or whether inclusion remains dependent on subsidy.

*Sources: [Monzo and Fair4All Finance pilot Flex Build card for excluded borrowers](https://www.electronicpaymentsinternational.com/news/monzo-and-fair4all-finance-pilot-flex-build-card-for-excluded-borrowers/) — Electronic Payments International*
